name: Cerium oxide
lead: Cerium oxide is investigated in skincare mainly as a mineral that could absorb UV light and as a source of antioxidant nanoparticles; people interested in protecting skin from photoageing and keeping a more even, youthful complexion follow this research.[1][8]

Cerium oxide (cerium(IV) oxide, ceria, CeO2) is a pale yellow-white, water-insoluble ceramic powder with a cubic fluorite crystal structure.[1] It is mainly an industrial material, used for glass polishing, glass decolourising, catalysts including automotive catalytic converters, and fuel cells.[1] In cosmetics discussions it appears as a candidate mineral UV absorber; Wikipedia describes nanoceria as a prospective replacement for zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in sunscreens because of lower photocatalytic activity.[1]

Most of the scientific literature concerns cerium oxide nanoparticles (nanoceria) as redox-active materials that mimic antioxidant enzymes, and their toxicity. No human trials of cerium oxide as a sunscreen or appearance product were found.

paras: Cerium oxide is widely used for chemical-mechanical polishing of glass and optics (hobbyists call it opticians' rouge), to decolourise glass, in catalytic converters and oxidation catalysts, in solid oxide fuel cells and in welding electrodes.[1]

Nanoceria has been proposed as a sunscreen ingredient because it absorbs UV and shows lower photocatalytic activity than zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.[1] A comparative study of TiO2, ZnO and CeO2 nanoparticles found that the three differed in cellular toxicity mechanisms, with ZnO acting largely through dissolution and CeO2 showing low toxicity in the test system.[2]

Ceria readily and reversibly shifts between Ce3+ and Ce4+ states, forming oxygen-deficient lattices.[1] Nanoceria has been reported to mimic superoxide dismutase and catalase, with activity depending on the cerium redox state,[3][4] and its protein adsorption and cellular uptake depend on surface charge.[5] A review has discussed its pharmacological potential,[6] and a 2006 study reported that rare-earth nanoparticles prevented peroxide-induced retinal degeneration in rat cells.[7]

A 2006 review of nanoparticle antioxidants described cerium oxide and other nanoparticles as potent and possibly regenerative free-radical scavengers in vitro and in vivo, covering neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory and longevity-related findings.[8] Later reviews discuss nanoceria as a versatile biomedical material, including as a radioprotective adjuvant in cancer treatment and as a component of nanotherapeutic agents for diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.[9][10][11] A 2024 review covers metal-based nanoparticles for cardiovascular disease.[12]

The 2008 comparative study reported that ZnO nanoparticles were toxic to cells through dissolution, whereas CeO2 was not, in the models used.[2] Wikipedia lists a low NFPA health rating for bulk cerium oxide and notes nanoceria has been investigated for antibacterial and antioxidant activity.[1] Safety of nanoceria applied to human skin has not been established by clinical studies found here.

Cerium(IV) oxide, also called ceria or cerium dioxide, is a pale yellow-white, water-insoluble powder with a fluorite crystal structure. Its distinctive property is that it reversibly loses oxygen at high temperature to form an oxygen-deficient state, a redox cycling that underlies its catalytic and polishing uses. [1] It occurs naturally as the mineral cerianite-(Ce), and cerium is mined mainly from bastnaesite and monazite alongside other rare earths. [1]

Its main industrial use is chemical-mechanical planarisation: it replaced iron oxide and zirconia for polishing glass and optics and is known to hobbyists as opticians' rouge. [1] It is also used to decolourise glass, in catalytic converters, self-cleaning oven walls and gas mantles, in solid oxide fuel cells, and in tungsten welding electrodes introduced to the US market in 1987. [1]

In appearance contexts, interest centres on cerium oxide's use as a sunscreen candidate and as an antioxidant material. Nanoceria is also a prospective sunscreen ingredient, proposed as an alternative to zinc oxide and titanium dioxide because of its lower photocatalytic activity. [1] Its antioxidant-like redox behaviour is the main reason for research interest in skin protection. [3][6][10]

Cerium oxide nanoparticles have been studied as antioxidant and antibacterial materials in cells and animals, with reviews describing radical-scavenging 'nanomedicine' applications and radioprotection. [6][8][9][10] Wikipedia notes a study reporting that cerium dioxide nanoparticles induced apoptosis and autophagy in human blood monocytes, and toxicity studies describe effects that depend on particle redox state and size. [1][2][3][15]

No studies found of cerium oxide as a sunscreen or on skin appearance. Human experiments with nanoceria in other settings are small: a pilot study randomized nine discarded human livers during four hours of machine perfusion, five of them treated with nanoceria, to assess uptake, distribution and efficacy against ischemia and reperfusion injury,[13] and a 2025 randomized trial examined systemically administered cerium oxide nanoparticles on oxidative stress in young patients with gingivitis and obesity.[14] A DNA-damage study of cerium dioxide nanoparticles has also been published.[15] Other research is laboratory and animal work on antioxidant activity and toxicity.

card.summary: Industrial ceramic oxide floated as a low-photoreactivity mineral UV absorber; antioxidant nanoceria research exists, sunscreen evidence does not.
card.note: No human sunscreen studies found; nanoceria safety on skin not established.

quick.overview:
Cerium oxide is a pale powder mostly used to polish glass and in catalysts. It has been suggested as a sunscreen ingredient because it absorbs UV with less photoreactivity than zinc or titanium oxide.

Most of the research is on nanoparticle versions and their antioxidant-like behaviour, not on skin protection in people.
quick.mechanism: Ceria flips between Ce3+ and Ce4+ states, which lets nanoparticles mimic antioxidant enzymes in the lab. Its UV absorption comes from the semiconductor-like oxide lattice.
quick.risks: No human sunscreen trials were found. Laboratory work shows low cell toxicity in some models, but nanoparticle safety on skin has not been clinically established.

chain: Ceria absorbs UV with low photoreactivity
Nanoceria scavenges reactive oxygen species in the lab
Possible less photodamage and a more even complexion
angle.text: Cerium oxide is discussed as a candidate sunscreen filter and antioxidant that could limit sun-related skin ageing, which affects tone and wrinkles. These uses are at the investigational stage.
